WELCOME    TO    PARLIAMENTARY    DELEGATION    FROM 
GHANA 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, I have an announcement to make. 
We have with us, seated in the Special Box, members of a parliamentary 
delegation from Ghana, currently on a visit to our country, under the 
distinguished Leadership of His Excellency, Mr. Peter Ala Adjetelely, 
Speaker of the Parliament of Ghana. 
On behalf of the Members of the House and on my own behalf, I take 
pleasure in extending a hearty welcome to the Leader and other members of 
the delegation and wish our distinguished guests an enjoyable and fruitful 
stay in our country. We hope that during their stay here, they would be able 
to see and learn more about our parliamentary system, our country and our 
people, and that their visit to this country will further strengthen the friendly 
bonds that exist between India and Ghana. Through them, we convey our 
greetings and best wishes to the Parliament and the friendly people of Ghana.

WRITTEN ANSWERS TO STARRED QUESTIONS  
Welfare of Tribals 
*301. SHRIMATI SARLA MAHESHWARI:  
SHRI A. VIJAYA RAGHAVAN: 
Will the Minister of TRIBAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that grants for the welfare of tribals were distributed 
to NGOs which were virtually non-existent; 
(b) if so, the methodology adopted to scrutinize the legitimacy of these 
organizations while granting funds; 
(c) whether Government initiated any action against the authority 
concerned for such corrupt practices; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF TRIBAL AFFAIR S (SHRI JUAL ORAM): (a) and 
(b) No, Sir. As per procedure laid down, proposals from NGOs are to be 
recommended by Collector of the district and sent to the Ministry by the 
State Government recommending the proposal, on the basis of the past 
performance of the organizations. 
The Ministry also examines the proposal on the basis of the Annual Reports 
of the organizations and satisfies itself about the ability of the organization to 
implement the project, before sanctioning it. 
(c) to (e) Wherever such instances co me to the notice of the Ministry, the 
State Governments are asked to take necessary action for recovery of the 
grants previously released and initiating criminal action.

VRS in PSEs 
*302. SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA: Will the Minister of HEAVY 
INDUSTRIES AND PUBLIC ENTERPRISES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are coming up with another round of Voluntary 
Retirement Scheme for staff of Public Sector Enterprises; 
(b) the number of surplus staff in different PSEs; 
(c) the estimated amount to be paid to separating employees; and 
(d) the other details in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF HEAVY INDUSTRIES -AND PUBLIC 
ENTERPRISES (SHRI MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) to (d) The Voluntary 
Retirement Scheme (VRS) was recently modified as per OM No. 2(32)/97-
DPE(WC)GL-LVI dated 6th November, 2001. These modifications were 
necessitated on humanitarian consideration to give a reasonable ex gratia to 
employees of PSEs where pay scales were not revised after 1.1.1987 or 
1.1.1992 and also to offer a reasonable ex gratia package to younger 
employees through the option of Gujarat pattern. No futher modifications are 
contemplated for the present. 
Rightsizing of manpower is an ongoing process. The staff requirements 
depend on the economic environment, market share, technology, shop floor 
practices etc. and the quantum of surplus staff, in any PSE, is likely to vary 
from time to time. The VRS is designed to give a reasonable support to 
voluntarily retiring employees. It is the decision of CPSEs to offer VRS and 
the timing thereof or the extent of rightsizing. It is not advised centrally by 
the Government.

Outbreak of Plague in H.P. and Haryana 
*306. PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a team of experts has been deputed by his Ministry to 
investigate the outbreak of plague in Himachal Pradesh and Haryana; 
(b) if so, whether the team has submitted its Report; 
(c) if so, the findings of the Report; and 
(d) the efforts made by his Ministry to  check the spread of plague in 
these States and to other parts of the country? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C. P. 
THAKUR): (a) to (d) After receiving in formation from Health Secretary, 
Government of Himachal Pradesh regarding admission of a few cases 
presenting with fever and haemoptysis (blood in sputum) in two hospitals of 
Shimla district and Post Graduate Institute of Medical Education and 
Research (PGIMER), Chandigarh, a team of experts from National Institute 
of Communicable Diseases (NICD), Delh i, consisting of an Epidemiologist, 
a Microbiologist and an Entomologist was deputed immediately to visit the 
affected areas of Shimla district fro m 14th to 17th February, 2002, for 
investigating the outbreak and to provide technical guidance to the State 
Government for containing the outbreak. Another team consisting of six 
public health experts was sent to Chandigarh on 22.2.2002. These teams 
visited the affected areas and examined the patients in the hospitals. 
After the visit, the teams submitted their report, which confirmed the 
outbreak of febrile illness with haemoptys is (blood in sputum) reported in 
Hatkoti Village of Jubbal-Kotkhai Block, Shimla District, as pneumonic 
plague. Out of the sixteen cases of pla gue detected in Himachal Pradesh and  
the  four  suspected  cases  with  plague  like  symptoms  from 
9 

RAJYA SABHA [15 April, 2002] 
Chandigarh and its adjoining areas, 5 have died and 15 have been discharged 
after recovery. 
The   following   steps   were   taken   to   contain   the   outbreak   in 
coordination with the State Government: 
1. The emergency medical requirements of the Government of Himachal 
Pradesh were promptly met with. 
2. Guidelines were issued to Health Authorities of Government of Himachal 
Pradesh, Uttaranchal, Punjab., Haryana and UT of Chandigarh on the 
following issues:     
• Strengthening of surveillance 
• Chemoprophylaxis to contacts 
• Quarantine  of close  contacts  restriction  of movement  of persons 
in affected areas 
• Standard work precautions 
• Safe disposal of bodies of persons dying due to plague 
 
3. Door to door interaction with the population in the affected and adjoining 
village for dispensing antibiotics, obtaining information about the new cases 
and educating the people was conducted. 
4. Fumigation of the patients' houses as well as the transport vehicles was 
carried out using Formalin (10%). 
5. About 28,000 to 30,000 people, including doctors, para-medical personnel 
and health workers were provided with chemoprophylaxis. 
6. Proper treatment of patients and isolation of cases in the hospitals. 
7. Quarantine of close contacts. 
8. EEC campaign focusing on restriction of mobility, immediate reporting to 
health facility in case of fever etc. and reassuring the public not to panic.

Sale of Profit making Industries 
†*307. SHRI JANESHWAR MISHRA: Will the Minister of 
DISINVESTMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government arc considering to sell those 
industries to the private institutions which arc earning profit and are the 
backbone of the economy of the country, under pressure from foreign investors; 
(b) if so, the total number of such companies which Government propose to sell 
despite their earning profit alongwith details thereof; 
(c) whether Government propose to sell National Fertilizer Limited, 
which is earning profit to the private sector; and 
(d) if so, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF DISINVESTMEN T (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) 
No, Sir. Decision to disinvest is based on considerations like classification of 
industry as strategic or non-strategic and not on considerations like profitability. 
Disinvestment in profitable or non-profitable public enterprise is aimed at optimal 
utilisation of capital, better corporate governance, reduction in commercial risk 
of tax-payers' money, release of scarce resources for deployment in social sectors 
like family welfare, health, education and other sectors of greater public interest. 
Disinvestment of the Government stake in PSUs is carried out in accordance 
with the declared policy of the Government and through a transparent process 
involving competitive bidding, which ensures that the best price determined by 
the market forces is obtained for the stake being disinvested. There is no 
pressure at all from foreign investors. 
(b) Disinvestment process has been going on in respect of 32 companies, out 
of which as per latest Public Enterprises Survey (2000-2001), the companies with 
net profit are: — Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd., Braithwaite & Co, 
Engineers India Ltd., Engineering Project (India) Ltd., Hindustan Petroleum 
Corporation

[15 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Amendment in the Family Courts Act 
*312.  SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: 
SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: 
Will the Minister of LAW, JU STICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Committee on Empowerment of Women 
has asked Government to amend the Family Courts Act; 
(b) if so, the recommendations of the Committee; 
(c) the details of States which have establish family courts; 
(d) the details of States which have not, so far, constituted family courts; 
and 
(e) the reasons for not establishing the same? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW, JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS 
(SHRI ARUN JAITLEY): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The Comimttee on 
Empowerment of Women in its Fifth Report on 'Functioning of Family 
Courts' has made a number of recommendations on amendments to the 
Family Courts Act. The Committee has, inter alia, recommended that the 
effectiveness of the Act should be assessed in the light of the shortcomings 
pointed out by the Committee. Such assessment should cover a review of the 
implementation of the Act, as also an evaluation of the substance of the Act 
and its limitations and the changes and modifications which are necessary to 
activate the Family Courts and to make their work fruitful and meaningful.

2216. SHRI MAN MOHAN SAMAL: Will the Minister of

THE MINISTER OF DISINVESTMENT (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) 
and (b) Yes, Sir. Disinvestment proc ess is an ongoing process and each 
transaction has to go through an elaborate process of participative decisions 
making, i.e. elaborate consultations with the concerned administrative 
Ministries and stakeholders. For various reasons like market conditions, 
financial performance of the companies under consideration, terms and 
conditions of sale, interest of the bidders, time taken for due diligence by the 
interested parties etc. the completi on of the disinvestment exercise may 
overshoot the 
32 

[15 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA

classification of industry as strategic or non-strategic and not on 
considerations like profitability. Disinvestment in profitable or non-profitable 
public enterprise is aimed at optimal utilisation of capital, better corporate 
governance, reduction in commercial risk of tax-payers' money, release of 
scarce resources for deployment in social sectors like family welfare, health, 
education and other sectors of greater p ublic interest. It is always ensured 
that the best price determined by the ma rket forces is obtained for the stake 
being disinvested. It is a fact that Government of India does not disinvest in 
distress to meet any deadlines. Under the circumstances, the companies 
earmarked for disinvestment in earlier ye ars are carried over to the next year 
disinvestment plan and annual receipt s may fall much short of the annual 
targets. For all these reasons, the receipts obtained during the period of Ninth 
Five Year Plan have fallen short of the target.

Population Policy 
2226.   DR. KARAN SINGH: 
SHRI AIMADUDDIN AHMED KHAN (DURRU): 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that though India adopted a population control in 
1950s, there has been no effective check on the rate of growth of poulation 
over the last 25 years; 
(b) whether any special plan of action has been or is being worked out 
since the population crossed the 100 crore mark; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) the contemplated population policy for the Tenth Five Year Plan? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (d) "No population control 
policy" was adopted in 1950's. However, India started a national programme 
emphasizing family planning to the extent necessary for reducing birth rates 
"to stabilise the population at a level consistent with the requirement of 
national economy". After 1952, sharp decline in death rates were, however, 
not accompanied by a similar drop in birth rates. 
The census figures of the last four decades indicate a perceptible decline in 
recent years, in the growth rate of the population of India. 
44 

[15 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA  
Decade Growth Rate 
1961—71  2.20% 
1971—81  2.22% 
1981—91  2.14% 
1991—01  1.93% 
While in absolute terms the population of India has increased by 180.6 
millions during the decade 1991-2001, however, the change in net addition 
has shown a steady declining trend starting from 1991. Undoubtedly a 
combination of the population momentum and the method mix widely 
adopted for fertility regulation has ensured that the net additionally is on the 
decrease. 
India adopted a comprehensive and holistic National Population Policy 
(NPP) in February 2000 with clearly ar ticulated objectives, strategic themes 
and operational strategics. Certain National Socio Demographic Goals to be 
achieved by 2010 have been formulated with the objective of achieving 
population stabilisation in the country by 2045.

Sale of spurious drugs in the market 
2238. MISS MABEL REBELLO: Will th e Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of flooding of spurious drugs in the 
market in Delhi; 
(b) the reasons for the markets getting flooded with sub-standard drugs; 
and 
(c) the action taken by Government in respect of part (a) above and for 
implementation of the existing laws regarding manufacture of drugs and the 
monitoring machinery made more effective in curbing the manufacture and 
marketing of spurious and sub-standard drugs in 
the country? 
 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) and (b) Government is aware of 
the problem of manufacture and sale of spurious drugs. This is a clandestine' 
activity indulged in by some unscrupulous and anti-social persons. As per 
the feed back available from Drugs Control Administration, Government of 
NCT of Delhi, out of the 743 test repo rts of drugs received during the period 
1.4.2001 to 31.3.2002. 11 drugs were reported to be spurious and 26 drugs 
were reported to be substandard. Besides, during the period 2001-2002, 1476 
survey samples were also collected  by Drugs Control Administration. 
Government of NCT of Delhi from licensed retail chemists through decoy 
customers/watchers for quick screening of active ingredients. 1475 samples 
have been tested but none was reported as spurious. It is not a fact that the 
market in Delhi is flooded with substandard or spurious drugs. 
(c) Under the provisions of Drugs and Cosmetic Act, 1940 and Rules 
thereunder. State Government have been empowered to enforce quality of 
drugs including check on manufacture or sale of spurious drugs. The said 
Act was amended in 1982 to provide for specific definition of spurious drugs 
and severe penalties extending to life imprisonment have been prescribed. 
59 

RAJYA SABHA [15 April, 2002] 
State Governments have been advised from time to time to provide adequate 
enforcement machinery and drug testing facilities and to keep strict 
surveillance over the inter-State move ment of spurious drugs facilities of 
Central Government testing labs have also been made available to the States 
for testing of drugs besides financial assistance provided to them to augment 
and strengthen their testing capabilities. 
The Drugs Controller General (India) has advised the State Drugs 
Controller to take the following measures for curbing the incidence of spurious 
drugs:—  
(i) Constitution and reactivation of State Drug Advisory Committees in 
which various trade and industry a ssociations as well as consumer 
associations should fine representation. Government of NCT of 
Delhi has constituted such a committee which consists of 
representatives of Indian Medical Association, Delhi Medical 
Association, All India Small Scale Pharmaceuticals Manufacturers 
Association (Delhi Branch), Chem ists Association and Voluntary 
Consumer Forums. 
(ii) Establishment of separate intelligence-cum-legal machinery with 
police assistance. 
(iii) Training should be provided to selected officials of Drug Control 
Administration in the modalities of intelligence work, prosecution 
etc. in respect of spurious counterfiet drugs. 
(iv) To ensure speedy analysis of drug samples by establishing own 
State level drug testing facilities. 
(v) State Drugs Control Authorities should be cautions while approving 
licenses for drug product to ensure that look-alike products are not 
encouraged. 
(vi) To develop efficient communication facilities and recall 
procedures. 
(vii)  To undertake surveillance of suspected dealers. 
60 

[15 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(viii) To engage experienced counsel for fighting spurious drug cases. 
(ix) To obtain cooperation of pharmaceutical industry by regular interaction 
with them. 
(x) To collect survey samples under National Survey Quality 
Evaluation of Drug (NSQED) Programme. 
In addition the following steps have been taken 
1. Association of Pharmaceutical Industry and All India Organisation of 
Chemists and Druggists have been asked to take necessary initiative to 
collectively combat the menace of spurious drugs. 
2. The problem of manufacture and sale of spurious drugs and to ensure its 
checking has been specifically expl ained to State Health Ministers 
during the meeting of Central Council of Health and Family Welfare. 
3. The Union Minister of Health and Family Welfare has constituted a 
Committee under the Chairmanship of DGHS on July 18, 2001 associating 
members from industry, trade, drug regulatory officials and public 
representative to go into all aspects of the menace of spurious drugs and 
suggest remedial measures.

2266. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO:  Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) the steps taken/proposed to be taken by his Ministry to promote the 
Two-Child Norm in pursuance of achieving the average total fertility of 2.1 
by the year 2010; 
(b) whether any meeting of the Chief Ministers of all States has been held 
or proposed to be held for arriving at  some consensus so as to achieve the 
goal; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) The National Population Policy 
adopted by Government of India in February, 2000 advocates for adoption of 
small family norm. The Family Welfare Programme in India is voluntary in 
nature, which enables a couple to adopt the family planning, methods, best 
suited to them, according to their choice, without any compulsion. They free 
to decide about the size of the fa mily. Therefore, the policy of the 
Government is to promote small family norm without prescribing for any 
number of children. In order to achieve the average total fertility of 2.1 by 
the year 2010, Government has decided to address child survival issues, 
maternal health issues and contraception issues simultaneously and 
effectively. It is only when children are healthy and their longevity is 
assured, those parents begin considering limiting the size of family. In turn, 
the health of the mother is key in ensuring the survival and well being of 
children. For these reasons, the Family Welfare Programme seeks to address 
these three issues simultaneously.

2267. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that according to the recent survey conducted by 
specialized group including experts belonging to UNAIDS and WHO 
revealed that the AIDS in the country is on decline; 
(b) if so, the details of the survey;  
(c) the effective steps his Ministry is taking to reduce the deadly disease 
to the minimum level; and 
(d) the steps, the NACO is taking to educate the people with regard to 
AIDS in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (d) As per the analysis of HIV 
Sentinel Surveillance data 2001, it is estimated that there are 3.97 million 
HIV infections in the country. The estimated number of adults living with 
HIV in India for 1998, 1999 and 2000 were 3.5 million, 3.7 million and 3.8 
million respectively. The estimated number of added infections since the last 
round of surveillance is" 110,000 compar ed with 160,000 in the previous 
year. 
In order to prevent and control of HIV/aids, a comprehensive Programme 
is currently under implementation throughout the country as a Centrally 
sponsored scheme. The main components consist of:- 
>  Reducing  the   spread   of  HIV  in   groups   at   high   risk   by 
92 

[15 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
identification of target populations and providing peer counselling, 
condom promotion, and treatment of sexually transmitted infections. 
>   Preventive intervention for the general population by Information, 
Education and Communication (IEC) and awareness campaign, 
provision of voluntary testing and counselling, safe blood transfusion 
services and prevention of occupational exposure. 
>    Providing financial assistance for opportunistic infections, home and 
community based care. 
>    Strengthening effectiveness and technical, managerial, financial 
sustainability at National, State and Municipal levels. 
Promoting collaboration amongst 'public, private and voluntary sectors. 
Awareness campaigns are an essential component of the prevention 
strategies adopted in the National AI DS Control Programme Phase-II. The 
Information, Education & Communication (IEC) strategy in NACO is 
operationalised at two levels. At the national level, implementation of the 
IEC strategy involves political and media advo cacy, social mobilization, 
creation of a supportive environment that reduces social stigma and 
discrimination for better access to services. 
At the State level Information, Education and Communication (IEC) 
activities are being undertaken by the State AIDS Control Societies to 
respond to local priorities and communication in local languages.

Ignoring the alert on Plague outbreak 
2269. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether alert on Plague outbreak was ignored by certain quarters; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the action taken to instruct State Governments to tighten vigil to stop 
spreading the menace? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C. P. 
THAKUR): (a) to (c) Immediately on receipt of information on 13.2.2002 
from Government of Himachal Pradesh regarding admission of a few cases 
presenting with fever and haemoptysis (blood in sputum) in two hospitals of 
Shimla district and Post Graduate Institute of Medical Education and 
Research (PGIMER), Chandigarh, a team of experts from National Institute of 
Communicable Diseases (NICD), Delhi consisting of Epidemiologist, 
Microbiologist and Entomologist was deputed immediately to visit the affected 
areas of Shimla district from 14th to 17th February, 2002 for investigating the 
outbreak and to provide technical guidance to the State Government for 
containing the outbreak. Another team consisting of six public health experts 
was sent to Chandigarh on 22.2.2002. These teams visited the affected areas 
and examined the patients in the hospitals. 
The following steps were taken to contain the outbreak in coordination 
with the State Government: 
>  The emergency medical requirements of the Government of Himachal 
Pradesh were promptly met with. 
>  Guidelines were issued to Health Authorities of Government of Himachal 
Pradesh, Uttaranchal, Punjab, Haryana and UT of Chandigarh on the 
following issues: 
—  Strengthening of surveillance 
—  Chemoprophylaxis of close contacts 
—  Quaratine of close contacts 
97 

RAJYA SABHA [15 April, 2002] 
—  Restriction of movement of persons in affected areas 
—  Standard work precautions 
—  Safe disposal of bodies of persons dying due to plague. 
>  Door to door interaction with the population in the affected and 
adjoining village for dispensing antibiotics, obtaining information 
about the new cases and educating the people was conducted. 
>    Fumigation of the patients' houses as well as the transport vehicles was 
carried out using Formalin (10%). 
>    About 28,000 to 30,000 people, including doctors, para-medical personnel 
and health workers were provided with chemoprophylaxis. 
>    Proper treatment of patients and isolation of cases in the hospitals. 
>   Quarantine of close contacts. 
>   IEC campaign focusing on restriction of mobility, immediate reporting 
to health facility in case of fever etc. and reassuring the public not to 
panic. 
Prevalence of Anaemia among children and women 
2270. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that about 3.5 million people in the country suffer 
from micronutrient deficiency leading to iron deficiency with anaemia 
prevalence among children and women; and 
(b) if so, the steps Government propose to take to improve the nutrition 
and help the lower strata of society? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) and (b) As per the National 
Family Health Survey 1998-99, 52 per cent women and 74 per cent children 
between age 6—35 months were found to be anaemic. A specific programme 
to combat anaemia in pregnant wome n and children is under implementation 
as a component of Reproductive   and   Child  Health   (RCH)   Programme.   
Under  this 
98 

[15 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
programme, every pregnant women is given 100 tablets of iron/folic acid 
(large) for prevention of anaemia. Pregnant women who are anaemic are 
given an additional 100 tablets. Anaemic children are provided with 100 
tablets of iron/folic acid (small). 
Several steps have been taken to improve nutritional status of women and 
children. These include, the Integrated Child Development Scheme which 
provides supplementary nutrition to young children and pregnant and 
lactating mothers. Promotion of exclusive breast-feeding up to six months of 
age and appropriate feeding practices is being undertaken. In addition, to the 
programme for control of iron deficiency anaemia a programme for control of 
Vitamin-A deficiency in children is under implementation. 
Setting up of an integrated disease surveillance network 
2271. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY:  Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have drawn up a plan to set-up an 
integrated disease surveillance network throughout the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether a pilot project is being set-up initially on a trial basis; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) by when, the full scheme is likely to be put in place? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (e) As a Public Health 
measure, Government of India has been implementing various National 
Health Programmes, including the National Surveillance Programme for 
Communicable Diseases. The Nati onal Surveillance Programme for 
Communicable Diseases was launched as a pilot programme in 1997-98 in 5 
districts (one each in Kerala, Karnatak a, Rajasthan, Haryana and Gujarat) 
with a view to strengthen the disease surveillance system so that early 
warning signals of outbreaks are recognized and appropriate follow-up 
action is  initiated.   The   programme   is   being  implemented   through   the 
99 

RAJYA SABHA [15 April, 2002] 
existing health infrastructure and surv eillance system involving training of 
medical and para-medical personnel, upgradation of laboratories, and 
improvement in communication system. The programme is currently being 
implemented in 100 districts. 
Under the Tenth Five Year Plan, a Project Implementation Plan, integrating 
various activities under the programme is under preparation so as to 
strengthen the existing surveillance system  at the district, State and National 
levels and to build up additional capacities for effective communication and 
technology, upgradation of laboratories etc., ensure involvement of public 
and private sector institutions, private practioners and NGOs in the process of 
effective implementation of disease surveillance programme. This would 
integrate non-communicable diseases also in the programme, develop proper 
urban surveillance systems, and optimize the utilization of available resources 
and to bring about effective inter- sectoral cooperation among various 
agencies in the Health and Non-Health Sector.

Central Sector Scheme for setting up of village grain banks in tribal villages 
was launched in 1996-97 in selected areas out of the areas identified by 
Central Planning Committee (CPC) as a preventive measure against death of 
tribal people by providing a safeguard against fall in nutritional standards.

Sub: Guidelines FDI in development of integrated township including

Government vide Press Note No. 4 (2001 scries) permitted FDI up to 100 
per cent for development of integrated townships, including housing, 
commercial premises, hotels, resorts, city and regional level urban 
infrastructure facilities such as roads and bridges, mass rapid transit systems 
and manufacture of building materials. Development of land and providing 
allied infrastructure will form an integrated part of township's development. 
2. FDI in the development of integrated townships will be subject to the 
following guidelines: 
(i) The foreign company intending to invest shall be registered as an 
Indian company under Companies Act, 1956 and will henceforth be 
allowed to take up land assembly and its development as a part of 
Integrated Township Development. All such cases would be 
processed by FIPB on the recommendation of Ministry of Urban 
Development and Poverty Alleviation and other concerned 
Ministries/Departments. Ministry of Urban Development and 
Poverty Alleviation will develop an  exclusive cell to deal with 
such cases. 
(ii) The core business of the company seeking to make investment, 
should be integrated township development with a record of 
successful execution of such projects elsewhere.

RAJYA SABHA [15 April, 2002] 
(iii) The minimum area to be developed by such a company should be 
100 acres for which norms and standards are to be followed as 
per local by laws/rules. In the absence of such bylaws/rules, a 
minimum of two thousand dwelling units for about ten thousand 
population will need to be developed by the investor. 
(iv) The investing foreign company should achieve clear milestones 
once their proposal has been approved. 
(a) The minimum capitalisation norms shall be US$ 10 million 
for a wholly owned subsidiary and US$ 5 million for joint 
ventures with Indian partner/s. The funds would have to be 
brought in upfront. 
(b) A minmum lock-in period of three years from completion of 
minimum capitalisation shall apply before repatriation of 
original investment is permitted. 
(c) A minimum of 50% of the inte grated project development 
must be completed within a period of five years from the date 
of possession of the first piece of land. However, if the 
investor intends to exit earlier due to reasons beyond his 
control, it shall be decided by FIPB on case-to-case basis.

development charges, external development charges and other 
charges as laid down in Master Plan/By laws, preparation of 
layout and building plan, development of internal and peripheral 
development, development. of other infrastructure facilities 
including the trunk services etc., will be the responsibility of the 
investor as per planning norms and standards on similar lines as 
those applicable to local invest ors. In the absence of such 
standards and norms, every State Government may decide their 
own conditions for which the Urban Development Plan 
formulation and implementation guidelines circulated by the 
Ministry of Urban Development and Poverty Alleviation may 
service as a guiding principle.

stations, milk booths will be handed over free of cost to the

New Rent Control Act 
2354. SHRI RUMANDLA RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the 
Minister of URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY 
ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have decided to discard the Land Ceiling Act 
and introduce a new Rent Control Act; 
(b) if so, the main reasons for the same; 
(c) by when a final decision in this regard is likely to be Jaken; and 
(d) to what extent this new Rent Control Act will be useful?  
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI BANDARU 
DATTATRAYA): (a) The Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act was 
repealed in January, 1999 and this has no bearing on the Rent Control Act. 
188 

[15 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) and (c) The relation between a landlord and a tenant in the National 
Capital of Delhi are presently governed by the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958. 
This Act was amended in 1960, 1963, 1976, 1984 and 1988. In 1992 a Model 
Rent Control Legislation was formulated by the Central Government and 
circulated to State Governments to enable them to carry out necessary 
amendments to their prevailing rent control laws. In the light of the Model 
Law, it was decided to amend the rent control law prevailing in Delhi. As the 
amendments were extensive and substantial in nature, it was decided to 
repeal the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 and replace it by a new Act. 
Accordingly, the Delhi Rent Act, 199 5 was enacted in 1995. The new Act 
namely, Delhi Rent Act, 1995 has, however, not came into force so far 
primarily due to the representations received from tenants. The matter was 
examined again by the Government and it was decided in 1997 to carry out 
amendments in the Delhi Rent Act, 1995 before bringing it into force. 
Accordingly, the Delhi Rent (Amendment) Bill, 1997 was introduced in the 
Rajya Sabha on 28.7.1997. The Bill was then referred to the Parliamentary 
Standing Committee on Urban and Rural Development to examine and 
report. The Committee submitted Its report on 21.12.2000. The Government 
examined the Report of th e Committee and accepted all its 
recommendations. A notice for moving official amendments has also been 
given to the Secretary General, Rajya Sabha. After the Bill is passed by the 
Parliament and assented to by the Pr esident, the Act alongwith amendments 
will be brought into force. 
(d) On enactment, the Bill envisages to minimise distortions in the rental 
housing market and encourage the supply of rental housing both from the 
existing and the new housing stock.

Conversion of freehold scheme by DDA 
2364. SHRIMATI SAROJ DUBEY: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that orders for conversion of freehold scheme 
initiated by the DDA has been stopped since 31st March, 2000; 
(b) whether the orders for conversion of freehold have been revised 
raising the conversion charge 2.30 times of the notified rates; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) the number of conversion cases filed before 31st March, 2000, which 
are still pending with the DDA and by when, these will be disposed of? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI BANDARU 
DATTATRAYA): (a) to (c) No, Sir. The scheme of conversion of leasehold 
system of land tenure in Delhi into freehold 
201 

RAJYA SABHA [15 April, 2002] 
as announced by the Government in February 1992 is an open-ended Scheme. 
The scheme of conversion of residential properties from leasehold to 
freehold on 1987 market rates was extended upto 31.3.2000 and thereafter 
the conversion was to be allowed on payment of conversion charges to be 
calculated on the basis of notified market rates prevailing on the date of 
conversion. 
Pending revision of market rates, the Delhi Development Authority has 
taken an interim decision to invite applications for conversion of residential 
properties from leasehold to freehold on the market rates notified by the 
Government of India for the 2 years block 1998—2000 which works out to 
2.31 times of the rates as were applicable upto 31.3.2000. The conversion 
charges prescribed by the DDA are provisional subject to notification of final 
rates by the Government. 
(d) The DDA have reported that all the applications received prior to 
31.3.2000 have been cleared except 5,425 applications which are pending due 
to various deficiencies which have b een conveyed to the applicants. The 
finalisation of such cases is dependant on the receipt of demanded 
information/documents from the applicants.
